repentant

/rih-PEN-tuhnt/ - the stress falls on PEN · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Repentant means feeling and showing sincere regret for wrongdoing.

Repentant at last, the prankster spent his Saturday scrubbing every locker he had glitter-bombed.

Example

The tackle was late and everyone in the rink knew it. What they remember now is what followed: Joaquin skated straight to the injured keeper, hung his head through the whole apology, repeated it in front of the squad that evening, and benched himself for the final without being asked. Nobody doubted the regret was real, because everybody watched it cost him something.

Repentant is the exact word for Joaquin, because it means feeling and showing sincere regret for wrongdoing — both halves required. Remorseful covers the gnawing feeling alone, hidden or not; a repentant person puts the regret where it can be seen, in apology, amends, or changed conduct.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

remorseful: Remorseful means full of the gnawing feeling of regret, whether or not anyone ever sees it — the guilt can stay hidden for years. Repentant demands both halves: the regret must be felt and shown, in apology, amends, or visibly changed conduct.

apologetic: Apologetic means saying sorry, and the sorry can run no deeper than good manners — people are apologetic about a missed call or a bumped elbow. Repentant is far heavier: sincere regret for a real wrong, displayed and paid for, never just a courteous phrase in passing.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

unashamed: feels no sting at all over what was done

gloating: openly pleased with the deed instead of sorry

Where it sits · how far remorse turns into action — embarrassed → sorry → repentant

embarrassed vs. repentant: Embarrassed is far milder than repentant — the surface flush of being caught, cheeks hot, wishing the moment away, with none of the sincere regret that repentant requires.

sorry vs. repentant: Sorry goes further than embarrassed — the regret is real and gets said — but it stops short of repentant, which carries that regret into visible amends.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — re-

Prefix — re-: thoroughly (an intensifier)

Root — pent-

Root — pent-: to regret (Old French pentir, from Latin paenitere)

Suffix — -ant

Suffix — -ant: inclined to; showing

Put it together

Put it together: Re- (here an intensifier: thoroughly) + pent- (to regret) + -ant (showing) = showing thorough regret. This is re-'s quietest job, one Latin loved: not 'again,' not 'back,' just 'through and through.' The repentant regret what they did all the way down — and, crucially, let it show.

Use the root in a new word: penance

Use the root in a new word: penance: Penance is regret made visible — an act performed to show how sorry you are, pent-'s root at work.

Word Choice

formal / warm

Repentant does double duty: the regret is felt and shown — apology, amends, changed conduct. Remorseful stays inside the chest; apologetic can be mere politeness; repentant requires the display. Its unit-mates map the moral field: the reprobate feels nothing and repents of nothing, while reprove names the gentle correction that hopes to produce exactly this. If the wrongdoer has turned around and is visibly making it right, repentant is the word.
